doc.title: Jackie McLean — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Harlem youth, Monk and Bird, and Greensboro
title: Monk's character compared with Bud's
summary: McLean describes Monk as bright, aware and in a state of grace, unlike the helpless Bud.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: Talk about – you made a comparison between – someone else in the literature that I read – between Bud and Monk, and you’ve kind of, I think, described for us that Bud was kind of – had blinders on to the world, not of his own choosing, but as a result of all the things that he’d gone through. How was Monk’s sense of the world? Sometimes you would think that he was detached from the world too.

He was in a state of grace, but aware of things, aware of things political. It’s some kind of mother-wit that’s just not from picking up the paper every day and reading it, not like that, but something he got from somebody in his family. He was very bright. Plus Thelonious went to one of the most incredible high schools in New York, Stuyvesant, one of those schools you have to test into, to have high brilliance in mathematics and all that. So Thelonious was very bright. Went to a wonderful high school. He was – but still, he was in kind of a state of grace, doing whatever he felt like he wanted to do without giving too much thought to the results of something. But Bud was almost helpless at some points in his life, where he needed somebody to be there.
